name: French Normandy Revival

geography.hearth: Philadelphia's Chestnut Hill; Berkeley and Los Angeles, California

lineage.note: The picturesque, half-timbered, tower-centred wing of the parent style. Same offices and same roof logic; the difference is the tower and the timbering.
The claimed ancestor: the timber-framed and rubble farm buildings of Normandy, with their round dovecote and colombier towers.
The farm-court plan, the flared eave, and the segmental dormer.
The small manor register, invoked where the composition becomes formal enough to need one.

Genuinely blended. American half-timbering, steel casements, leaded glass and masonry veneer are shared wholesale with Tudor Revival; on many streets the two are separated only by the presence of a round tower.
Informal planning and the deliberate composition of irregular groups, transmitted through the same Anglo-American publishing channel that produced Tudor Revival.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The Norman farmhouse variant of French Eclectic, identified by a round or polygonal entrance tower with a conical roof set at the junction of two wings, combined with steep hipped roofs, half-timbering, and mixed brick, stone and stucco walls.
description.long:
French Normandy Revival is the one variant in this branch that can be identified from a moving car by a single element. The round entrance tower, capped with a conical roof and containing the front door and often a stair, sits in the inside corner where two wings meet, and it comes directly from the freestanding colombier - the dovecote tower - of the Norman farm court, which American architects and returning soldiers had photographed extensively and which they moved from the farmyard to the front door because it made a spectacular entrance.

Everything else follows the parent style. The roofs are steeply pitched hips, 12:12 and up, running at the same pitch on all faces, often flared at the eave. The walls mix materials with some freedom - brick, rubble stone, and stucco, with half-timbered panels in the gables and upper storeys, which is the point where this variant borrows heavily from Tudor Revival and where the two become genuinely difficult to separate. Windows are casements, tall and grouped. Dormers break the cornice line, arched or segmental. The plan is informal, usually an L or a shallow U, and where the composition is large it wants a walled forecourt.

Two developments define its American realisation. Robert Rodes McGoodwin's French Village at Chestnut Hill, built 1925-28 for George Woodward, is the East Coast case, executed in Wissahickon schist with real masonry and real restraint. William Raymond Yelland's Thornburg Village - universally called Normandy Village - at 1781-1851 Spruce Street in Berkeley, built in 1927 for the contractor Jack Thornburg, is the West Coast case and is considerably wilder: sagging ridges, hand-adzed timbers, carved corbels, and a deliberate air of medieval fantasy that shades into the Storybook manner then flourishing in Los Angeles. Between the two lies the whole range of the variant, from archaeology to theatre.

What it is like depends on which end you are at. At the Philadelphia end it is calm, grey, and heavy, and the tower reads as a legitimate piece of planning - you enter through it, turn, and arrive in a hall. At the Berkeley end the same tower is a stage set: the plaster is trowelled unevenly on purpose, the timbers have axe marks that were put there with an axe, and the whole group is theatrical in a way that is completely unembarrassed about itself. Both work. The failure mode is the middle - a suburban builder's box with a half-round clad turret glued to the front, which has neither the mass of the first nor the conviction of the second.

defining_characteristics: Round or polygonal entrance tower with a conical roof, set at the junction of two wings and containing the front door or a stair
Steeply pitched hipped roofs, 12:12 or steeper, at consistent pitch on all faces, frequently flared at the eave
Mixed wall materials - brick, rubble stone, and stucco - with half-timbered panels in gables and upper storeys
Casement windows, tall and grouped, with true divided or leaded lights
Dormers breaking the cornice line, arched or segmental-headed
Informal L- or U-shaped plan, ideally with a walled or partly enclosed entrance court
diagnostic_tells: The conical-roofed round tower at an inside corner is decisive; nothing else in American domestic architecture places one there.
Steep hipped roofs with no dominant front gable, plus half-timbering. Tudor Revival gives you the timbering with gables; the parent French Eclectic gives you the hips without timbering.
Wall material changes vertically and abruptly - stone below, stucco and timber above - at a floor line or a jetty.
Casements, not double-hung, and a segmental or round-headed dormer.

Against genuine Norman building: the original tower is a freestanding dovecote in a farm court and does not contain the house entrance; the original timber frame is structural and 4-8 in. thick; and the original farm is a group of buildings, not one house pretending to be a group.

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style is broader and usually calmer - it may be entirely symmetrical, is often all-masonry, and rarely uses half-timbering or a tower. This variant is the picturesque Norman end, defined by the conical entrance tower and by mixed timbered walls.

Roof geometry again. Tudor Revival is gabled and English-referenced; French Normandy Revival is hipped, flares its eave, uses casements, and puts a round tower at the entrance. The half-timbering and the masonry-veneer technology are shared, which is why the pair is so often confused.
The Cotswold variant is lower, all-stone, has no tower and no timbering, and rolls its eaves. The Norman variant is taller, mixes materials, uses timbering, and depends on the tower.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof-dominant, as in the parent style, with the tower as the compositional pivot: its diameter and height set the scale against which the two wings are judged, and its conical roof establishes the steepest pitch on the building.
typical_ratios: Tower diameter 9-14 ft; height to eave 1.1 to 1.4 times the adjacent wall height
Conical tower roof pitch 18:12 to 24:12 - steeper than the main roof by at least 4:12
Main roof pitch 12:12 to 16:12, constant on all faces; roof height 0.6-1.0 times wall height
Half-timber members 5-8 in. face width, spaced 16-30 in. clear, projecting at least 1 in. from the stucco plane
Casement leaf 16-22 in. wide by 40-56 in. high, grouped in twos and threes
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and grouped. Each wing carries its own loose rhythm of casement clusters; the tower interrupts both and is the only element on the composition that resolves anything.

massing_affinities.note: Two or more hipped wings of unequal height meeting at a tower.
The suburban builder reduction - a simple block with a turret and one steep hip.
Larger examples where the composition becomes formal enough to read as a manor.
The Norman farm court taken literally, with service ranges pulled into the composition.

constraints.statement: A round or polygonal tower, minimum 9'0" in diameter, capped with a conical roof at 18:12 or steeper, must be present at the junction of two wings and must contain either the entrance or a stair. A tower applied flat to a facade, or one narrower than 9'0", voids the variant.

test.note: Tests the tower's own conical roof pitch. Tower diameter (min 9'0" -- no matching vocabulary variable, tower_diameter_ft is missing) and 'must contain either the entrance or a stair' stay prose.

constraints.statement: Main roof pitch 12:12 to 16:12, constant within 1:12 across all faces, hipped. The tower roof must exceed the main roof pitch by not less than 4:12.

test.note: Tests the main roof pitch range. 'Constant within 1:12 across all faces, hipped' and 'the tower roof must exceed the main roof pitch by not less than 4:12' (no separate tower-roof-pitch variable exists to compute the cross-roof differential against) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Where half-timbering is used it must describe a plausible frame under the parent Tudor rule: continuous verticals from sill to plate, horizontals terminating at posts, braces at 45 degrees or steeper, members 5-8 in. wide projecting not less than 1 in. from the infill plane.
Vertical material changes must occur at a floor line, a water table, or a jetty, with a minimum 4 in. horizontal offset. Stone below and stucco above stopping mid-storey is forbidden.
Windows shall be casements with true divided or leaded lights, leaves 16-22 in. wide, grouped in twos and threes. Double-hung sash on principal elevations is forbidden.

exemplars.name: Thornburg Village (Normandy Village)
exemplars.note: William Raymond Yelland for Jack Wood Thornburg. The West Coast case at its most theatrical - hand-adzed timbers, sagging ridges, carved corbels - and a Berkeley landmark.

exemplars.name: French Village
exemplars.location: Chestnut Hill / Mount Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Robert Rodes McGoodwin for George Woodward, 1925-28. The East Coast case in Wissahickon schist, archaeological rather than theatrical.

exemplars.name: Oheka Castle
exemplars.note: Delano & Aldrich, 1914-19. Included as the grand French precedent from which the suburban Norman version is derived, with the same steep hipped roofs and tower motifs at estate scale.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Arrol Gellner and Douglas Keister, Storybook Style: America's Whimsical Homes of the Twenties (2001)
David R. Contosta, Suburb in the City: Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, 1850-1990 (1992)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)

proportion_packs.note: Secondary. The revival works in stone and half-timber together, and this pack holds only the first half -- the rubble field, the dressed quoins and jambs, the plinth. The timber-framed panels want the half-timber infill module that is still on WP-4.1's list, and until it exists this node's framed walling has no pack, which is worth stating rather than letting the stone binding imply coverage it does not have.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own proportional_system names the tower explicitly as 'the compositional pivot: its diameter and height set the scale against which the two wings are judged' - a textbook statement of the picturesque dominant-mass logic, and the tower's conical roof at 18:12-24:12 against a main roof of 12:12-16:12 is close kin to facade-picturesque's own gable_treatment and roof_form derived_rules. No classical order anywhere in the defining characteristics or constraints; unlike chateauesque and beaux-arts-american, this variant's own lineage carries no Beaux-Arts weight (its Ecole descent is inherited only at second hand through the french-eclectic parent) and no order is bound here for that reason.

The variant's own hard constraint (c03) requires that half-timbering, where used, 'describe a plausible frame under the parent Tudor rule: continuous verticals from sill to plate, horizontals terminating at posts, braces at 45 degrees or steeper' - a real structural-frame logic, not applied decoration, which is exactly what timber-bay's bay-and-post reconstruction encodes. Genuine gap flagged honestly: timber-bay's own applies_to list does not yet name this node (it names norman-vernacular, german-fachwerk, tudor, elizabethan and jacobean, but not this revival or its parent french-eclectic) - bound anyway because the fit is structurally direct and the omission reads as an oversight in the pack's applies_to curation rather than a deliberate exclusion.

The lineage record carries real weight here: 'arts-and-crafts-british, descends_from, weight 0.6 - informal planning and the deliberate composition of irregular groups' and a hybridizes_with edge to tudor-revival at weight 0.7, which is itself bound to trim-craftsman in this corpus (see tudor-revival's own applies_to entry on that pack). Chosen over trim-classical because nothing in this variant's defining characteristics, diagnostic tells or constraints calls for a classical order or an entablature-derived interior - the register is rustic timber and stone throughout, at both the Chestnut Hill (restrained) and Berkeley (theatrical) ends the style's own description names.

The node that states the pack's most important applied-work rule, and states it as a minimum rather than a figure: half-timber members '5-8 in. face width, spaced 16-30 in. clear, projecting at least 1 in. from the stucco plane'. That inch is what separates honest applied half-timbering from painted-on stripes -- without it there is no shadow, no depth and no reason for the timber to be there. Read it with the pack's projection rule and its construction-tolerance conflict, which is about the same problem from the other end: applied boards CAN be set dead true and usually are, which is why applied work so often reads as a printed pattern.

SCOPED BINDING (OQ 49, ruled 25 Aug 2026), and the first one authored. This node states `jetty-overhang`'s material-change rule almost verbatim -- 'vertical material changes must occur at a floor line, a water table, or a jetty, with a minimum 4 in. horizontal offset' -- and it has NO JETTY of its own. It names one as a permitted datum for something else, which makes it a CONSUMER of one rule and not an instance of the type. Before the `slots` field the only choices were to bind the whole pack, which would have made the corpus assert a framed overhang on a style that has none, or to leave the rule restated in the node, which is the duplication this library exists to remove. Scoped to `material_change_rule`, which the pack writes exactly once, so the node gets the offset rule and none of the fourteen about a cantilever it does not have.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes are wholly about a full classical order — a column of 20 modules, an entablature of 5 divided 3:3:4, a denticular cornice, acanthus rows and diagonal volutes — and it reaches this node from beaux-arts-american at cascade depth 3 with no lineage edge between them, to dimension door_surround and frieze. The node's own record has already adjudicated this exact question one layer down: it binds trim-craftsman over trim-classical on the stated ground that nothing in its characteristics, tells or constraints calls for a classical order or an entablature-derived interior, and its facade binding note says flatly that there is 'No classical order anywhere in the defining characteristics or constraints'. The register the node states for itself is rustic timber and stone, and its only cornice is an eave line dormers break, not an order's. Same shape as tudor-revival's chambers-ionic decline: a classical order arriving by descent to dimension members the style does not have.
declined_packs.quote: nothing in this variant's defining characteristics, diagnostic tells or constraints calls for a classical order or an entablature-derived interior
declined_packs.note: Governs 2 slots: door_surround and frieze. Declining passes both to palladio-tuscan (from italian-renaissance); 0 slots lose all dimensioning. Worth saying plainly: the decline stops THIS order and does not stop orders — the fallback is another classical pack, which is OQ 58's stated limit one layer down.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes describe a full classical order and nothing else — a column of 20 modules, an entablature of 5 divided 3:3:4, Vignola's Regola figures confirmed against Ware in diameters — dimensioning entablature, frieze, cornice, pilaster, door_surround and the interior trim run. The node's own facade binding note states flatly that there is no classical order anywhere in its defining characteristics or constraints, and its interior binding note gives the same ground for choosing trim-craftsman over trim-classical; the register it states for itself is rustic timber and stone, its only cornice an eave line that dormers break. This is the identical case the node has already decided against vignola-composite, arriving from the same beaux-arts-american at cascade depth 3 with no lineage edge between them. The contradiction is between the pack's stated subject and the node's own sentence, not between their names.

The other order packs already lost every address here to facade-picturesque, trim-craftsman, stone-course and timber-panel, so the decline records the judgment rather than moving a figure — and, as with the vignola-composite decline, it stops THIS order and does not stop orders.
